newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Momentum building for Annan as UN secretary-general.
newsitem.headline: Momentum building for Annan as UN secretary-general.

text.p: Kofi Annan, the Ghanaian head of peacekeeping operations, on Thursday tightened his grip on the post of U.N. secretary-general with France as the last holdout in a 14-1 Security Council vote.
Diplomats said Annan's score on the second informal poll meant that even Egypt, the chief backer of Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali, voted for the 58-year old Annan.
Several envoys discounted new compromise candidates being presented to the council at this time and said the remaining question was how to convince Paris to change its mind.
The diplomats said the final vote could be as early as Friday after the council takes another informal poll. "We are rapidly reaching the end game," said one council source.

The 15-member Security Council held two rounds of unofficial polls on Thursday meant to "discourage" or "encourage" four declared candidates from Africa, which is given preference in fielding nominees. Boutros-Ghali has stepped aside temporarily from the polling following a U.S. veto of his candidature.
To win, a candidate must have a minimum of nine votes and no veto from the council's five permanent members -- the United States, Russia, Britain, China and France.
Boutros-Ghali's five-year term expires on Dec. 31.

Annan's closest rival was Amara Essy, the foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and the 1994-95 U.N. General Assembly president. He received seven votes on Thursday, with two permanent members opposing him, the United States and Britain.

The other two candidates, Ahmedou Ould-Abdallah, a former foreign minister of Mauritania, who was once the U.N. envoy to Burundi, and Hamid Algabid, a former Niger prime minister and the secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference, fell far below the nine vote mark.

Said Council President Francesco Paolo Fulci of Italy: "The smoke coming out of the Security Council chimney this morning is once again black," a reference to the colour of the smoke after an inconclusive vote to elect a new pope.
"Up until this moment there are no new candidatures. Members of the council shall meet again to conduct more straw polls tomorrow," he said.
British U.N. envoy Sir John Weston, believed to be one of Annan's strongest backers, said: "That was a very encouraging discussion." He said developments were moving in a positive direction.
And France's ambassador Alain Dejammet said only that the next secretary-general would be an African. "We hope he will come from Africa and very likely, he will speak French."
All four candidates speak French but Annan is the only one from a English-speaking country.
The English-French language feud at the United Nations escalated when Washington on Nov. 19 vetoed Boutros-Ghali, a former Egyptian deputy prime minister, author and French-educated law professor.
U.S. officials maintained he was sluggish in reforming the world body, a position shared by few other countries, and particularly not by France, his chief backer when he won election five years ago.
In turn, the United States and Britain this week voted against or abstained on the poll for the three other francophone African candidates on the list, diplomats said.
Boutros-Ghali suspended his candidacy on Dec. 4 and could reactivate it any time. But he is believed certain to be vetoed again by the United States.
